c1.story:
In 1903 Jamsetji Tata opened the Taj Mahal Palace on the Mumbai waterfront. More than a century later, the company that runs it still owns the building, but most of the new Taj, Vivanta and Ginger hotels it adds each year belong to somebody else. Indian Hotels simply puts its name on the gate and collects a fee. That shift, from owning hotels to lending a brand to them, is the most important thing to understand about this industry, and it explains why the listed names behave so differently.

The first door is the owned hotel. EIH, which runs the Oberoi hotels, Leela, Chalet and Juniper own the land and the building, run the rooms, keep the whole room rate and carry the whole cost. When rates rise, almost every extra rupee drops to profit. When travel collapses, the cost stays. The building itself is a floor under the value: prime land in central Mumbai does not go out of fashion.

The second door is brand and management. Indian Hotels, ITC Hotels and Lemon Tree increasingly sign management contracts: an owner builds the hotel, the brand runs it and takes a fee on revenue and on profit. Very little capital, a steady fee in good years and bad, and growth that depends on how fast the company can sign new hotels.

The third door is the leveraged owner or platform. SAMHI, Ventive and their peers buy or lease hotels with borrowed money, run them under global brands like Marriott and Hyatt, and refinance as cash flow grows. It is the owned-hotel bet with a loan attached, so occupancy has to rise faster than the interest bill.

The fourth door is everything around the hotel: travel, leisure and food services. Travel Food Services feeding airport passengers, Thomas Cook selling holidays, Mahindra Holidays selling Club Mahindra memberships, Wonderla running theme parks.

Owners win biggest in a boom. Brands win in every phase. The market pays more for the second.
c1.read:
The four tiles are the four doors. Read each from top to bottom, then compare the bars.

  • The name and the line under it tell you who owns what: the land and the building, just the brand and the fee, borrowed hotels under a global flag, or the services that ride on travellers.
  • The tickers are listed names that mostly sit behind that door. Click one to open its stock page. Note that the big brands also own some flagship hotels, so a name like Indian Hotels straddles the first two doors; the tile shows where its growth is coming from.
  • The profit bar shows how much of each sale the company keeps. Brand and management sits at high: a fee with almost no cost attached. Owned hotels and travel services sit at medium. Leveraged owners sit at low, because interest takes a big slice before shareholders see anything.
  • The bet line is what you are really betting on: room rates beating costs, with property as a floor; signing hotels fast; occupancy beating interest; Indians travelling more.

Read the analogy underneath: the house owner, the broker whose name lets the owner charge more, the buyer on a big loan, and the taxi stand outside. Then the so-what: owners gain most when rates jump and bleed in a downturn, while brand companies earn less in a boom but keep earning in a bust. That is the whole reason the market gives the asset-light names a higher multiple.

c2.story:
A hotel night looks like a simple product: a bed, a shower, breakfast. Behind it is a five-station chain, and the slowest station decides the whole cycle.

The first station is land and building. A developer buys land in a city centre or a resort town, gets approvals and builds, typically over three to five years. City land is expensive and approvals are slow, so supply arrives late, long after the demand that justified it. This station is held by owners, real-estate groups and the government's own tourism corporation.

The second station is brand and distribution. A name and a booking engine bring guests in through websites, online travel agents and corporate contracts. Indian Hotels, ITC Hotels and Lemon Tree stand here, facing global chains, Marriott, Hilton and Accor, that compete for the same owners' signatures.

The third station is rooms and operations: housekeeping, the front desk, maintenance, every single night. The owned hotels and platforms, EIH, Leela, Chalet, Juniper, SAMHI, Ventive, stand here.

The fourth is food, banquets and leisure, and it is bigger than outsiders expect. In a large city hotel, restaurants, weddings and conferences can earn as much as the rooms. The same owners stand here, along with Travel Food Services at airports and Wonderla in theme parks.

The fifth is the traveller: business guests, wedding parties, domestic tourists and a smaller stream of foreigners.

When rooms cannot be added quickly, a rush of guests raises the price, not the room count.

That is the key insight of this kitchen. India has far fewer branded rooms per head than China or Thailand, concentrated in Mumbai, Delhi NCR, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and the leisure belts of Goa, Rajasthan and Kerala. When post-Covid demand surged, the first station could not respond for years, so room rates broke records instead. That is why this cycle has been so kind to owners.
c2.read:
Two layers: five stations on top, and a band row underneath showing who holds each.

The five boxes run from land and building on the left to the traveller on the right. Under each, read what happens and who stands there. Watch the cast: developers and owners on the left; Indian brands alongside Marriott, Hilton and Accor in the second box; the listed owners and platforms in the third; the same owners plus airport food and theme parks in the fourth; corporates, families and travel agents on the right.

The band row is the summary. The first cell is owners and developers. The second, India brands and global, is coloured as the rival station, because that is where the global chains compete head on with Indian brands for management contracts. The two coloured India listed cells sit under rooms and operations and under food, banquets and leisure. The last cell is travellers.

So the picture is this: listed Indian hotel companies are strongest in the middle, running rooms and banquets, while the global chains contest the brand station. An owner choosing a brand for a new hotel is choosing between Taj, ITC or Lemon Tree on one side and Marriott or Hilton on the other.

Use it when reading news. A new hotel announced is an event at station one, and it reaches room rates only years later. A management contract signed is an event at station two, and it adds fee income as soon as the hotel opens. A big wedding season is an event at station four, and it shows up in the very next quarter.

c3.story:
Ten years ago, if you asked who filled India's best hotels, the answer would have been foreign tourists and expatriate executives. Today the honest answer is your cousin's wedding, your colleague's offsite and your neighbour's long weekend in Udaipur.

Indian hotel demand has become overwhelmingly domestic, and it comes from several very different wallets.

Corporate travellers fill weekday city rooms and meeting spaces. Their numbers move with office hiring, especially in IT and banking, and with the return to office. A Bengaluru hotel's Tuesday night is a direct read on the city's tech economy.

Weddings and social events are the Indian peculiarity. A big wedding books banquets, room blocks and sometimes the entire property for days. Demand follows the auspicious dates on the calendar, so a season with fewer dates can thin a quarter regardless of the economy. Destination weddings have turned palaces in Rajasthan and resorts in Goa into year-round businesses.

Domestic leisure tourists drive weekends at hill stations, beaches and pilgrim towns, and they follow infrastructure. New highways and airports open new markets: the Ram temple in Ayodhya, consecrated in January 2024, turned a small town into a hotel-building destination almost overnight.

Conferences and events come in bursts. The G20 meetings across India in 2023 filled city hotels for months.

Foreign tourists still matter for luxury and heritage hotels, and they follow visas, the rupee and safety perceptions.

Around the hotel sit three more customers: air travellers buying airport meals, families buying timeshare memberships and theme-park tickets, and the holiday crowd booking packaged tours.

India's hotels are now filled by Indians. That makes the wedding calendar more important than the foreign arrivals chart.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read each in three lines: who, what they buy, what moves them.

  • The name identifies the wallet: corporate travellers, weddings and social events, domestic leisure tourists, conferences and events, foreign tourists, air travellers, families on holiday.
  • The middle line is what they buy, which tells you which part of the business they feed. Corporates fill weekday rooms; weddings fill banquets and room blocks; leisure fills weekends; air travellers feed airport food; families feed timeshares and theme parks.
  • The last line is the driver to watch: office hiring, the wedding calendar, long weekends and new airports, government summits, visa ease and the rupee, passenger traffic, school holidays.

A useful exercise is to sort the tiles by when they spend. Corporate demand fills Monday to Thursday; leisure fills Friday to Sunday; weddings cluster in the winter season. A hotel with a good mix of all three runs full more nights of the week and more weeks of the year, which is why city hotels with big banquet halls are so profitable.

Then note the so-what: demand is now mostly domestic. If you are tracking foreign tourist arrivals as your main hotel indicator, you are watching the smallest tile. Watch weddings, office travel and new airports instead.

c4.story:
Here is the beautiful, dangerous economics of a hotel: a room costs almost the same to run whether a guest sleeps in it or not.

Follow a hundred rupees of an owned hotel's revenue. Only a small slice, about an eighth, goes to food, fuel and guest supplies. The giant bite, about half, goes to staff, power, rent and brand fees, and most of that is fixed. The housekeeping team, the chef, the air-conditioning in the lobby all cost the same on a quiet Tuesday as on a sold-out wedding weekend. Then depreciation and interest take another slice about as large as the inputs, because the building is big and was often built with debt. What is left is roughly a quarter.

Now picture what happens when room rates rise. The staff are already paid. The power bill barely changes. So an extra rupee on the room rate falls almost straight to profit. That is operating leverage, and it is why hotel earnings can grow far faster than hotel revenue in an up-cycle. Unfortunately it works the other way too. In 2020, when Covid emptied hotels, revenue collapsed and most of the costs stayed.

A hotel is a cinema hall. Every extra ticket, and every extra rupee on the ticket, is almost pure profit.

The brand and management model looks different. Its input costs are tiny, about a twentieth, because it is mostly not running the kitchen itself. Its operating costs are similar in share, and its depreciation is lower because it does not own most of the buildings. What is left is a bit over a third of every rupee. And its fee line, the management fee on someone else's hotel, is nearly pure margin and grows with every signing.

The investor's starting number is revenue per available room, which combines how full the hotel is with how much each room fetches. Watch that first and margin second.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of revenue down to what is left: owned hotels on one side, brand and management on the other. Read each left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is food, fuel and guest supplies. It is small on both: about an eighth for owned hotels, about a twentieth for brand companies. In most industries this is the big bar; here it is not.
  • The opex bar is staff, power, rent and brand fees, about half the revenue on both charts. This is the fixed cost that creates operating leverage.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is twice as tall for owned hotels, because they carry the buildings.
  • The last bar is what is left: roughly a quarter for owners, a bit over a third for brand companies.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover for amounts.

Below the charts, the list marks which lines matter. Room rate and occupancy, employee and power cost, depreciation, capex, interest and management fees all get a yes. Rent and lease is marked sometimes, since leased hotels swap capex for a fixed rent that bites in a downturn. Working capital gets a no: guests pay at checkout.

The so-what tells you where to look first: revenue per available room growth, then margin. When rates rise on a fixed cost base, the margin follows on its own.

c5.story:
Most industry clocks on these pages turned in the last five years. The hotel clock turns slowly, over a decade or more, because the slowest part of the business, building a hotel, takes years.

The last complete cycle began in the mid-2000s. Business travel and foreign arrivals surged with India's growth story, and room rates in Mumbai and Delhi rivalled global cities. Developers did what developers do on cheap credit: they announced a flood of new hotels around 2008.

Then the hotels opened, into the global financial crisis. The November 2008 attacks on Mumbai, which targeted the Taj and the Oberoi Trident, hit travel confidence at the same time. Delhi's hotels built for the 2010 Commonwealth Games opened into empty markets. From 2009 to 2014, rates were crushed by too many rooms chasing too few guests.

What followed was the quiet bottom, roughly 2015 to 2018: almost no new supply, because nobody wanted to build after that experience. Occupancy crept back while rates stayed flat. By 2019, occupancy was finally near its old peak and rates had started to rise.

Covid then threw the clock off its hands. Hotels emptied in 2020, owners burned cash and took on debt. But the shock left the underlying setup intact: almost no new rooms had been built for a decade.

Covid was a shock, not a cycle. The supply drought underneath it was the real story.

When travel came back in 2022, it came back domestic and with a vengeance: revenge travel, delayed weddings, then the G20 year. Room rates broke through their old peak and kept going. 2024 set records, ITC spun off its hotels, and brand companies signed management contracts at a record pace. Rate growth has since cooled from the sprint, but is still rising. The new supply wave has been announced, but mostly for 2028 and beyond.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, clockwise from the top. Notice how long the arcs are in years: boom from 2005 to 2008, peak in 2008, bust from 2009 to 2014, bottom from 2015 to 2018. This is a long-cycle industry. The arrow sits in the boom arc, labelled mid-to-late up-cycle, with the detail that rates are rising and supply is still scarce. Hover an arc to read what defined it.

The timeline runs from 2019. Read the colours: neutral in 2019 as occupancy recovers, bust for 2020 and 2021 as Covid empties hotels, boom for 2022 and 2023 and again in 2024, then neutral in 2025 as rate growth slows from its sprint, and the latest entry marked now.

The four hands are what you watch to move the arrow.

  • Revenue per available room growth: high single digits, arrow up. If it slows below inflation, that marks the peak.
  • New branded room supply: low but rising, mixed. This is the hand that ended the last cycle, so it is the one to watch hardest.
  • Air passenger traffic: growing, arrow up.
  • Signings pipeline at brand companies: record, arrow up. That is fee income for years.

Three hands up and one mixed. The mixed one, supply, is the slowest-moving and the most dangerous, which is exactly why the so-what says rates can keep rising until today's announced hotels open.

c6.story:
If you could watch only two numbers for Indian hotels, you would watch how many people are flying and how many new rooms are opening. The cycle is simply the gap between them.

The first three-dot dial is domestic air passenger traffic. Most people who check into a hotel arrived on a plane, or at least the guests paying the highest rates did. More flyers means more hotel nights, and it also means more meals sold at airport food courts. New airports matter twice: Navi Mumbai's airport, which began commercial flights in December 2025, adds capacity to the country's most important hotel market, and every new regional airport opens a leisure destination.

The second three-dot dial is new hotel room supply, and it works against the industry. Each new hotel in a city competes for every guest, and enough of them cap room rates for everyone. This is the dial that ended the last cycle, and its readings arrive years in advance, because a hotel announced today opens in three or four years.

Then the two-dot dials. Corporate hiring and office occupancy decide weekday business travel. The wedding calendar and household wealth, which the gold price loosely tracks, decide banquets. Interest rates cut both ways: they hurt leveraged owners, but higher rates also slow new supply, which helps incumbents. GST on rooms and food shifts demand between price bands overnight. And security or geopolitical events can empty hotels for weeks.

Air traffic is the demand. New rooms are the price. Everything else is texture.

The one-dot dials are gentler. Crude oil raises airfares and dampens leisure trips. A weaker rupee keeps Indians holidaying at home and brings foreigners in. Food and wage inflation squeezes margins if room rates lag.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches the hotel's P&L. Notice the variety: travellers needing rooms, competition for guests, weekday business travel, banquets, debt cost, the guest's final bill.
  • A rise does: green up helps, red down hurts, a diamond cuts both ways. Interest rates carry the diamond: bad for leveraged owners, good for incumbents because they slow new supply.
  • Weight: one to three dots.

The last column shows today's reading where we track a matching series: the Nifty IT index as a proxy for corporate hiring, gold for household wealth, the money-market rate, Brent crude, the rupee, general CPI and India VIX as a stand-in for security shocks. The two most important dials, air traffic and room supply, show a dash; you follow them through aviation data and company announcements.

Read the three-dot rows first. They point in opposite directions, air traffic green and room supply red, which is the whole cycle in two lines. As long as the green one grows faster than the red one, rates rise.

Then scan the red two-dot rows. GST and security events are the ones that can turn a quarter without warning. The so-what line beneath the table repeats the lesson: the cycle is the gap between air traffic and new supply.

c7.story:
The bottlenecks in this industry are unusual: some of them are the reason it is so profitable right now.

Start with scarce city land. A plot large enough for a hotel in central Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru is rare and expensive. That keeps new supply slow, which hurts anyone trying to expand, but protects anyone who already owns a hotel there. It is a two-sided bottleneck, and in this cycle the incumbents are on the right side of it.

Then slow approvals, which are structural. Building permits, fire safety, liquor licences and environment clearances each take time, so supply responds to demand years late. Again: frustrating for builders, gold for owners.

The recurring bottlenecks are the ones that hurt. Shocks to travel come without warning. The November 2008 Mumbai attacks, the 2020 pandemic, regional conflicts: each can empty hotels overnight while the fixed cost base keeps running. Seasonality is gentler but constant. The winter wedding and holiday season is strong, the monsoon quarter weak, and one quarter is never a trend. Tax and liquor rules differ by state and change overnight. A bar is high-margin until the state raises excise or delays a licence renewal.

The slow bottleneck is people. Chefs, managers and front-desk staff are poached by every new hotel and by cruise lines, and wages rise as supply rises.

And the cyclical one is the one that ends booms: debt-funded supply waves. When financing is cheap and room rates are high, many owners build at once. It happened before 2008, and the hotels opened into a bust.

Slow land and slow approvals stretch the up-cycle. Cheap money and a building rush are what end it.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites, and a severity label. Here, unusually, several rows help the listed incumbents, so read the labels carefully.

  • Two-sided: scarce city land. It slows everyone's expansion but protects the hotels already built. In this cycle, it is a tailwind for owners.
  • Structural: slow approvals. Permanent, and again mostly protective of incumbents, because it keeps new supply late.
  • Recurring: shocks to travel, seasonality, and tax and liquor rules. These are the quarter-level surprises. Shocks are the dangerous ones because the cost base does not shrink; seasonality is predictable and should not be over-read.
  • Cyclical: debt-funded supply waves. This is the row that ends the cycle, and it connects to the interest-rate dial in the wiring diagram.
  • Slow: skilled staff shortage, a gradual wage pressure that rises with every new hotel.

The so-what under the table is the summary: the first two rows stretch the up-cycle, while a travel shock or a debt-funded supply wave is what ends it.

A useful habit: when you read about a hotel company announcing a big expansion, ask whether it is adding to the supply wave in the cyclical row, or signing management contracts on hotels someone else is building. The second carries far less of that risk.

c8.story:
Hotels look like a lightly regulated business. In practice, a hotel's price, its bar and its pace of growth are all set by officials, often at the state level.

Start with tax. The GST Council sets the tax on room tariffs and restaurant bills by price band, which means a slab boundary can shift demand between hotel classes overnight. A guest will happily book the room priced just under a threshold rather than just over it. In 2025, the Council cut the GST rate for mid-priced rooms, which the rulebook marks as live: it changed the arithmetic for the mid-priced segment where Lemon Tree, Ginger and many branded business hotels compete.

Then liquor. State excise departments license bars and set duties, and bar revenue is some of the highest-margin money a hotel makes. Every state has different rules, and they change with state budgets.

Then the pace of supply. Municipal and fire authorities issue building permits and safety approvals, and their speed decides how fast new hotels open. That makes them, quietly, the most important regulator for the cycle.

The Ministry of Tourism handles star classification, tourism campaigns and infrastructure status, which lets qualifying hotel projects borrow on better terms. FSSAI licenses and inspects kitchens, and a food safety lapse is a reputational hit that travels fast. Visa policy shapes foreign arrivals for luxury hotels. Airport operators award food and lounge concessions, which are long but re-tendered, which matters a great deal to Travel Food Services.

In hotels, the regulator who matters most for the cycle is the one issuing building permits.

The one to watch for the future is SEBI's REIT framework. Office and retail REITs already list in India. If hotels get bundled into listed trusts, owners gain an exit route that could re-rate owned hotel portfolios.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care, and its status.

  • Always: the Ministry of Tourism, state excise departments, municipal and fire authorities, and FSSAI. These are permanent fixtures. The municipal and fire row matters most for investors, because it sets the pace of new supply, the second three-dot dial from the wiring diagram.
  • Live: the GST Council, visa and e-visa policy, and airport operators. The GST row is the one that can shift demand overnight between price bands. Airport concessions matter specifically for airport food and lounge operators.
  • Coming: SEBI's REIT rules for hotels. A slow but potentially large change for owned-hotel portfolios.

Notice what is missing: there is no row marked new, and no rule here that dictates room prices. Hotels set their own rates every night, which is part of why pricing power is so strong in an up-cycle.

Then notice the split by door. Owned hotels and leveraged owners are most exposed to the excise, municipal and GST rows, because they run the bar, the building and the bill. Brand companies are more insulated: their fee is on revenue, whatever the tax. Travel and food services are most exposed to the airport and visa rows.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Run Porter's five forces over Indian hotels today and you get an unusual result: neither business is under heavy pressure on any spoke. That is what a supply-constrained up-cycle looks like.

Take rivalry. In each micro-market, say Mumbai's airport district or central Bengaluru, only a handful of branded hotels compete. They watch each other's rates, but with occupancy high, nobody needs to undercut. Brand companies face a different rivalry: they compete with Marriott, Hilton and Accor for an owner's signature on each new hotel.

Suppliers are mostly staff and land, both scarce. Owners feel wage and power inflation directly. Brand companies barely do; it is the owner's payroll, not theirs.

Buyers are fragmented. Large corporates negotiate annual rates, and online travel agents take a commission, but no single guest has much leverage, and in a tight market even corporates pay up.

Entrants are where the two doors differ most. For owners, land, approvals and years of construction keep newcomers out. For brands, entry is easier: a new brand can sign an existing hotel and put its name on the gate tomorrow. That is why brand companies score a little higher on this spoke.

Substitutes exist at the budget end, homestays, serviced apartments and Airbnb, but not in luxury hotels or in banquet halls. Nobody holds a five-hundred-guest wedding in an Airbnb.

When supply is scarce, the hotel sets the price. The forces only bite when the new rooms arrive.

The so-what follows: owners keep most of the profit in this phase, while brand companies keep a steadier slice in every phase. The market's preference for asset-light names is a bet that phases change.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: owned hotels and brand and management. The first thing to notice is how small both shapes are. No spoke reaches the outer ring for either. Compare this with almost any other industry page and you see why hotels are so profitable right now.

Then look for the differences, because they are small but telling.

  • Rivalry: the two shapes match, a moderate score for both.
  • Supplier: owned hotels reach slightly further. They carry wage and power inflation; brand companies do not.
  • Buyer: the shapes match, low for both. Guests are fragmented.
  • Entrants: here the brand shape reaches further, the one spoke where it is worse off. A new brand can sign existing hotels; a new owner must build.
  • Substitutes: owned hotels reach slightly further, as homestays nibble at the budget end.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason.

Use the chart as a stress test. Imagine the supply wave arriving: the rivalry and buyer spokes would push outward for owners first, since they carry the fixed cost. A brand company's fee would shrink a little with rates, but its shape would barely change. That asymmetry is why the call prefers asset-light names.

c10.story:
Hotel results calls are refreshingly direct. Managements quote the same handful of numbers every quarter, and eight of them tell you nearly everything.

The headline number is revenue per available room. It is occupancy multiplied by the average rate, so it captures both how full the hotel is and how much each room fetches. Then split it: average room rate is pricing power, and you want it rising faster than inflation; occupancy is how full the hotels are, and above a certain level, managers stop chasing volume and start pushing price. In this cycle, rate has done most of the work.

Then EBITDA margin, which shows operating leverage at work. When revenue per room grows on a fixed cost base, margin expands without anyone having to cut anything.

For brand companies, the most important forward-looking number is signings and pipeline: hotels signed but not yet open. Each one is fee income for years, arriving with almost no capital.

Employee cost to sales is the discipline check. Wages are the biggest fixed cost and they rise with every new hotel competing for staff.

Then the survival numbers. Debt to EBITDA tells you whether an owner can sit through a shock like 2020. Most large brands paid down debt after Covid; the leveraged platforms carry more. And ROCE tells you whether the buildings earn their cost of capital, which for an owned hotel on expensive city land is harder than it looks.

Revenue per room tells you about the cycle. Debt to EBITDA tells you whether you survive the next shock.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of each company. The first three rows, revenue per room, rate and occupancy, are a family: the first is the product of the other two.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures, as rules of thumb. Some split by door. EBITDA margin and ROCE have separate bars for owned hotels and asset-light companies, with asset-light expected to earn a much higher return on capital because it uses so little.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of the listed companies. Four rows have one: EBITDA margin, employee cost, debt to EBITDA and ROCE. The operating rows, revenue per room, rate, occupancy and pipeline, come from investor presentations and show a dash.

A caution: the medians blend hotel owners with airport food operators, quick-service restaurant franchisees and travel companies in the listed universe. Compare a hotel owner's margin with the owned-hotel good mark first, and treat the median as context.

The best routine each quarter is to read revenue per room growth against inflation, then margin, then debt. If revenue per room growth slows toward inflation while margins stop expanding, the cycle's arrow is moving toward the peak.

c11.story:
The warnings for hotels arrive on unusually long and predictable schedules, because the biggest risk, new supply, is announced years before it opens.

Start with what speaks now. Domestic air passenger traffic is a same-quarter signal: travellers check in the same week they fly. Monthly aviation data is the closest thing to a real-time hotel demand index in India.

One quarter out, the signals cluster. Booking pace on online travel agents fills next quarter's rooms. The wedding season calendar, with its auspicious dates, decides banquet revenue. Office leasing and IT hiring tell you about weekday business travel a quarter ahead.

Two quarters out sit airport capacity additions. A new terminal or a new airport opens a leisure market, and the hotels around it fill as the flights start.

And then there is the dot furthest to the right, three quarters or more: new hotel openings announced. This is the signal that ended the last cycle, and it gives you the longest warning of any. A hotel announced today caps rates in its city years from now. Right now the visible supply wave is mostly slated for 2028 and beyond.

Combine the main signals and you get the three-sign rule. The up-cycle is healthy when revenue per room grows faster than inflation, new supply grows slower than demand, and air traffic is rising. All three are ticking today: revenue per room in the high single digits, the supply wave years away, and air traffic growing steadily.

Three ticks with premium multiples means the earnings have to keep coming. The market has already paid for the story.

That is the logic behind the call: prefer asset-light brand names and city owners with low debt, and be wary of leveraged owners priced for perfection.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to see its channel into earnings.

  • Same quarter, far left: domestic air passenger traffic. Your real-time demand gauge.
  • One quarter ahead: booking pace on online travel agents, the wedding season calendar, and office leasing with IT hiring.
  • Two quarters ahead: airport capacity additions.
  • Three or more quarters ahead, far right: new hotel openings announced. This lone dot on the right is the most important one on the chart, because it is how the last cycle ended.

Use the chart as a reading order, right to left. First check the supply dot: is the pipeline of announced hotels in your companies' cities getting bigger? Then airports, then bookings and weddings, then confirm with air traffic.

Below the chart is the rule with three signs. All three carry ticks: revenue per room beating inflation with high single-digit growth, supply growing slower than demand with the wave years away, and air traffic rising steadily. Three of three is the healthiest reading the rule can give.

Then the call box: the headline, three points, and what would change it: a travel shock, a supply wave arriving sooner than expected, or a sharp slowdown in corporate travel. The second of those is the one the rightmost dot on the chart will warn you about first.
